overview: Haida Gwaii is the island homeland of a continuing Haida nation, not a vanished kingdom. The imported outline omits the southern archipelago and extends north toward Alaska; it is not a reliable boundary of Haida Gwaii. Examples below identify their own places and dates.

periods.title: Island communities
periods.summary: Haida communities drew on sea and forest resources and maintained skilled traditions of making.

periods.title: Colonial disruption
periods.summary: Disease devastated village populations during the nineteenth century.

periods.title: Cultural renewal and recognized title
periods.summary: Haida institutions and recent title agreements are chapters in continuing nationhood.

sections.title: A village, a forest and the sea

items.text: At SG̱ang Gwaay, south of this map’s incomplete outline, remains of large wooden houses stand beside memorial and mortuary poles. These are traces of a nineteenth-century village. The carved figures record family histories and responsibilities, not simply decoration for an empty landscape.

Deep deposits of discarded shells at the same site record a much longer history of eating and living there. Salmon and shellfish were important foods; red cedar supplied houses, canoes and carved poles. Different traces connect meals, transport and public monuments.

A bentwood box begins with carefully cut grooves in a single plank. Steam softens the wood so its sides can turn at the corners. The technique combines precise measurement and knowledge of wood, four walls do not necessarily require four separate boards.

Museum box VII-B-560, made by 1901 or earlier, stored eulachon oil. The catalogue notes that its wood remains saturated with the oil. This is unusually direct evidence of use: a beautiful carved container also preserves traces of an important food and trade product.

The crest carved on that box refers to inherited rights and its owner’s identity. Haida designs are not a collection of interchangeable public logos. An object’s appearance can carry information about relationships and authority as well as the maker’s artistic skill.

A spruce-root hat in the Canadian Museum of History, VII-B-892, dates to 1884 or earlier. Its maker used different twining methods on crown and brim. The fine root strands and consistent pattern reveal substantial preparation and patient, controlled handwork.

The museum describes women learning weaving from mothers, aunts and grandmothers. Experienced weavers can recognize individual habits in the way a hat is finished. A family skill can carry knowledge too subtle to fit into a short written instruction.

Haida weaver Ariane Xay Kuyaas explains choosing straight spruce roots of suitable, consistent sizes, then preparing them before weaving. Planning starts in the forest, not at the first stitch. Running short of matching material halfway through would be a frustrating kind of homework.

The Haida Gwaii Museum’s 2021 catalogue prints “Haawa, haw’aa” alongside “thank you” in its acknowledgements. These are attested contemporary written forms, reproduced from a specific publication. Haida has regional dialects; a modern written expression is distinct from the visual language of a carved crest.

The Haida Gwaii Watchmen programme began in 1981 with volunteers protecting old village sites. Watchmen stay at sites and share knowledge with visitors. Caring for places includes explaining why houses and poles remain connected to families whose ancestors lived there.

In April 2024, the Haida Nation and British Columbia signed the Rising Tide agreement recognizing Haida Aboriginal title. Implementation was arranged in stages. Recognition within Canadian law is a development in an ongoing relationship, not the first moment Haida people possessed a homeland.

A separate agreement with Canada, signed in December 2024 and publicly announced in February 2025, recognized Haida title to lands including the intertidal area. Its terms preserve private-property interests and public services while jurisdictions are reconciled through a transition period.

ending.text: Epidemics and colonial policies disrupted villages and families, but Haida nationhood continued. Recent title agreements and community stewardship demonstrate ongoing authority and responsibility. The 1500 endpoint is only a map interval; it is not an ending for Haida people.
